questions.question_text: Which of these is **not** a real number?

options.why: Read the minus sign as though it were under the root; here it sits outside, giving the real value $-2.236\ldots$
Treated a root that does not simplify as undefined, but $5$ is positive so the root is real.
Applied the even-index rule to an odd index; a cube root of a negative number is real.

questions.solution_text:
Squaring a real number never gives a negative result, so nothing real multiplies by itself to give $-5$.
The index is even and the number under the root is negative, so $\sqrt{-5}$ is not real.

questions.question_text: Evaluate $\sqrt{121}$, giving a single whole number.

options.why: Gave both solutions of $x^{2}=121$, but the root symbol names only the positive value.
Chose the negative square root, although $\sqrt{\;}$ always gives the positive one.
Halved $121$ instead of finding the number that multiplies by itself to give $121$.
Dropped the minus sign written in front of the root.
Halved $144$ and applied the minus sign instead of taking the square root.
Treated the minus sign in front of the root as though it were under the root.

questions.solution_text:
The minus sign sits outside the root, so take the root first.
$-\sqrt{144}=-(12)$
$=-12$

questions.question_text: Which of these is a real number?

options.why: Ignored that the index $4$ is even, so nothing real raised to the fourth power gives $-81$.
Assumed a familiar perfect square stays real once the minus sign is under the root.
Used the odd-index rule because $64$ is a perfect cube, but the index here is the even number $6$.

questions.solution_text:
The index $3$ is odd, so a negative number under the root is allowed.
$(-10)\times(-10)\times(-10)=-1000$
$\sqrt[3]{-1000}=-10$

options.text: $\sqrt{0}=0$, and $0$ is the only number with a square root of $0$.
$\sqrt{0}$ is undefined, because $0$ is not positive.
options.why: Extends the $x<0$ rule to $x=0$; the root is undefined only for negative numbers.

options.text: $\sqrt{0}=1$, because anything to the power $0$ is $1$.
options.why: Confuses a zero index with a zero under the root sign.
Carries the two-solutions idea across from $x^{2}=0$, which in fact has the single solution $0$.

questions.solution_text:
$0\times0=0$, so $\sqrt{0}=0$.
No other number squares to give $0$, so this root has exactly one value.

options.why: Moved the minus sign under the root, where it makes the expression not real.
Left off the minus sign in front of the root, giving the positive root instead.
Kept a minus sign under the root as well as in front; the inner one still makes the root not real.

questions.solution_text:
The minus sign sits outside the root, so take the root first.
$-\sqrt{36}=-(6)$
$=-6$

questions.question_text: $\sqrt{p+2}$ is a real number and $p$ is an integer less than $3$. Which list gives every possible value of $p$?

options.why: Required $p+2$ to be strictly positive, dropping the value that gives the real root $\sqrt{0}=0$.
Applied the not-negative condition to $p$ itself instead of to the expression $p+2$ under the root.
Included $p=3$, although $p$ must be less than $3$.

questions.solution_text:
The number under the root must not be negative.
$p+2\geq0$
$p\geq-2$
Combining that with $p<3$ for integers gives $p=-2,-1,0,1,2$.

questions.question_text: $\sqrt{a-7}$ is a real number. Which value of $a$ is **not** possible?

options.why: Assumed $\sqrt{0}$ is undefined, but $7-7=0$ and $\sqrt{0}=0$ is real.
Overlooked that $11-7=4$ is positive, so the root is real.
Assumed the largest value must fail, but $20-7=13$ gives a real root.

questions.solution_text:
The number under the root must not be negative.
$3-7=-4$
That is negative, so $\sqrt{a-7}$ is not real when $a=3$.
